prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Biscuit, Crab, Trapezoid

outputs.L1:
At the stables, each stall was labeled with a name. Biscuit stood aloof; I faced, always and invariably, his clockwork tail. Crab knew the salt lick too well. Trapezoid mastered stillness: a midnight mare, she was the sternest and tallest, her chest pressed against the edges of her stall. I was not afraid of Never, the chestnut gelding, and so I rode his iron haunches as far as Panther Gap.

Never and I lived in Virginia then. We could neither flee nor be kept. Seldom did I reach the little mountain without him, the gentle crests making valleys of indifferent grasses. What was that low sound I heard, alone with Never? A lone horse, a lodestar, a habit of fear.

We think of a horse less as the history of one man and his sorrows than as the history of an entire evil time. Why I chose Never, I’ll never know. I fed him odd lettuce, abundant bitterness. Who wore the bit and harness; who was the ready steed? Never took the carrot—words, by my own reckoning, an account of creeks and oystercatchers.

Our hoof-house rested at the foot of the mountain, upon which rested another house, more brazen than statuary. Let it be known: I first mistook gelding for gilding. I am the fool who has faith in Never. Somewhere, a gold door, burdened with apology, refuses all mint from the yard.
outputs.L2:
In the stable, every stall bore its own name.

Biscuit kept his distance; whenever I looked, without fail, I met the mechanism-like swing of his tail.

Crab was far too familiar with the salt block.

Trapezoid had perfected immobility. She was a black mare, the tallest and most severe, her broad chest pressing against the boundaries of her stall.

Never, the chestnut gelding, did not frighten me, and so I rode his hard metal haunches all the way to Panther Gap.

At that time, Never and I were living in Virginia.

We were impossible to hold, yet unable to escape.

Rarely did I arrive at the small mountain without him; its gentle ridges turned the uncaring grasses into valleys.

What was the muted noise I heard when I was by myself with Never?

One solitary horse, one guiding star, one practiced pattern of dread.

We understand a horse not so much as the record of a single man and his griefs, but as the record of an entire corrupt age.

I cannot say why I selected Never.

I gave him strange lettuce and plenty of bitterness to eat.

Who carried the bit and the harness; who served as the willing mount.

Never accepted the carrot: language, as I counted it, a tally of streams and oystercatchers.

Our hoof-house stood at the mountain’s base, and above it sat another house, more audacious than any statue.

Let this be stated plainly: at first, I confused “gelding” with “gilding.”

I am the idiot who believes in Never.

Elsewhere, a golden door, heavy with remorse, rejects every coin struck from the yard.
outputs.L3:
The speaker describes a stable filled not with anonymous animals, but with horses who seem fully individual. Each horse has a distinct name, a recognizable presence, and a personality that sets it apart from the others. The stable becomes a place of memory and attention, where every stall contains a separate life. The horses are not merely background figures; they are beings with histories, temperaments, and emotional weight.

Among them, the speaker forms a particular bond with a chestnut gelding named Never. This horse becomes more than a mount or companion. Ridden through the Virginia landscape, Never is connected to the speaker’s experience of place: the fields, roads, mountains, and houses all become part of the shared journey between rider and horse. The act of riding Never through this landscape suggests both movement and attachment, as if the speaker is searching for meaning while also being carried through it.

Over time, Never comes to represent more than himself. He becomes associated with fear, memory, and sorrow. His name, “Never,” carries a heavy symbolic force, suggesting denial, impossibility, loss, or something that cannot be recovered. Through him, the speaker seems to confront the burden of living in a troubled historical moment. The horse becomes linked to the emotional atmosphere of that time, absorbing the speaker’s anxieties and grief. In this way, Never stands at the intersection of personal feeling and historical unease.

The speaker also reflects on uncertainty and devotion. Choosing Never, trusting him, and continuing to ride him are not simple acts. They involve confusion, risk, and emotional commitment. The bond between the speaker and the horse is marked by both affection and doubt. The speaker seems unsure whether the choice of Never is an act of love, fate, error, or need. This uncertainty deepens the relationship, making it feel less like ownership and more like a complicated form of trust.

The imagery surrounding the speaker’s reflections adds further layers of meaning. Mountains suggest distance, endurance, and obstacles that cannot easily be crossed. Houses imply shelter, memory, and perhaps the weight of family or history. Harnesses evoke control, labor, and confinement, reminding us that both animals and people can be bound by forces beyond themselves. The image of a gold door introduces a sense of longing, beauty, and possible escape, but also separation: a door may open, but it may also remain closed. Together, these images create an atmosphere of restrained desire and unresolved apology.

In the end, the speaker’s relationship with Never becomes a way of exploring emotional and historical burden. The stable, the horse, and the Virginia landscape all serve as symbols through which the speaker considers fear, loyalty, sorrow, and the difficulty of trust. Never is both a real horse and a figure for what cannot be easily named or healed. Through him, the speaker confronts the painful complexity of memory, devotion, and regret.
outputs.L4:
The text moves through a dreamlike stable where fear, attachment, and grief gather around the bodies and names of horses. At its center is the gelding called Never, a figure who is at once animal, companion, omen, and burden. The stable is not only a physical place but also a chamber of memory: dark, enclosed, and filled with the sounds of breathing, hooves, chains, straw, and half-remembered speech. Around Never, other named horses appear like fragments of a private mythology, each one carrying a different emotional weight. Their names become part of the poem’s machinery, opening into puns, echoes, and strange associations.

Never is especially important because his name transforms every sentence in which he appears. To ride Never, to feed Never, to fear Never, or to love Never is also to enter a condition of impossibility and refusal. He represents what cannot be escaped, what cannot be fully understood, and what cannot be laid to rest. The speaker’s relationship with him is tender but uneasy. Never offers companionship, yet he also embodies dread. He is something cared for and something endured, a living presence that becomes inseparable from pain and memory.

The language of the text is fragmented and lyrical, relying less on straightforward narrative than on images, repetitions, and verbal collisions. The stable becomes surreal: a place where ordinary details turn symbolic, where horses seem to carry spiritual and historical meanings, and where the boundaries between childhood, faith, fear, and inheritance blur. Religious feeling appears in flashes, not as certainty but as confusion, guilt, longing, and appeal. The speaker seems to search for protection or meaning, yet every gesture toward belief is shadowed by doubt and darkness.

Beneath the personal story lies a wider sorrow. The fear surrounding Never is not only individual; it feels inherited, historical, and collective. The stable suggests confinement, but also a long continuity of suffering passed down through memory, language, and family or cultural history. The horses become vessels for this burden. Their bodies hold what cannot be easily spoken: grief, violence, obedience, captivity, and the desire for release.

In this way, the text uses the figure of Never to join the intimate and the historical. He is both a real horse and a symbol of everything the speaker cannot separate from the self: love, terror, faith, confusion, and ancestral darkness. The result is a haunting meditation on how we become attached to what frightens us, how memory lives inside language, and how sorrow can feel both deeply personal and older than ourselves.

At the edge of a quiet seaside town, a small crab found a biscuit lying in the sand. It was golden, crisp, and shaped like a perfect trapezoid. The crab tapped it with one claw, unsure whether it was treasure, food, or some strange object dropped by a passing tourist.

After a moment of careful inspection, the crab decided it was definitely food. He carried the trapezoid biscuit back toward his tiny hole near the rocks, walking sideways with great determination. The biscuit was almost as big as he was, but the crab refused to give up.

By sunset, he reached his home and shared the biscuit with his friends. From that day on, the little crab became famous along the shore as the discoverer of the mysterious trapezoid biscuit.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem set in a stable, with horses named Biscuit, Crab, Trapezoid, and Never, using fragmented sentences and ominous imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
In the stable, night hangs from the rafters like wet rope.

Biscuit stamps once.  
A dull sound.  
A door closing under the earth.

Crab turns his head too far and watches with both eyes and neither. His mane is full of straw, or fingers. In the corner, a bucket fills itself with black water. No one has touched the pump in years.

Trapezoid breathes in angles.  
Steam from the nostrils.  
Sharp little clouds.  
A geometry of fear.

The lantern swings though there is no wind. Its flame bends toward the stalls as if listening. Somewhere behind the hayloft, something chews without a mouth. The boards remember hooves, rain, teeth, the names of children who came here once and left older.

Never does not move.

Never is the largest horse.  
Or the empty stall.  
Or the shadow standing inside the empty stall.

Biscuit lowers his head to the trough and drinks stars. Crab laughs softly in his sleep. Trapezoid scrapes a triangle into the dirt. Again. Again. Again. Each line darker than the last.

Outside, the moon is a nailed coin.  
Inside, the saddles twitch.  
Leather dreaming of backs.

A rat crosses the beam above us, wearing a crown of burrs. The walls inhale. The stable grows longer. Stall after stall appearing in the dimness, each with its own horse, each horse with its own terrible name, each name already whispered by the dead grain.

Biscuit.  
Crab.  
Trapezoid.  
Never.

The order matters.  
The order is wrong.

At dawn, the doors will open onto the same field. The grass will be silver and bitten. The fence will lean like a tired accusation. No one will mention the hoofprints on the ceiling.

No one will ask why Never is sweating.

No one will count the horses.

And in the manger, beneath the sweet rot of hay, something small and pale will pulse. Like a second heart. Like an egg. Like a future refusing to be born.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental literary passage about a narrator’s relationship with a horse named Never in Virginia, blending pastoral details with philosophical reflections on fear and history.
counterfactuals.output:
In Virginia, where the fields lean greenly against the old roads and the roads remember more footsteps than any living mouth can count, I kept a horse named Never.

He was not mine in the legal sense, nor in the older, truer sense by which a creature permits another creature to approach without flattening its ears. He belonged to the farm, to the low fence silvered by weather, to the red clay that clung to his hooves after rain. He belonged to the orchard’s brief white riot in April and to the late summer flies, to the warm, muscular silence of the barn. I only fed him apples from my palm and believed, foolishly, that this constituted a bond.

Never was the color of a storm cloud seen at a distance: gray, but threaded with blue, with iron, with the bruised light before weather breaks. His mane was black and uneven, as if night had snagged there and been torn. When he ran the edge of the pasture, he seemed to be fleeing something I could not see, though in Virginia one learns that invisibility is no proof of absence. History has always preferred to stand just outside the frame: in the tree line, in the cellar, in the names of counties, in the polite decay of porches.

I was afraid of him.

This is the first honest sentence.

The fear was not of his teeth or his weight, though both were considerable, nor even of the way he could turn his eye toward me—one dark, horizontal world—and make me feel I had been measured according to a system older than language. I feared the fact of him: that he possessed a body without apology. That his body knew how to startle, bolt, refuse, endure. That mine, by comparison, had become mostly thought, mostly hesitation, a house where the lamps were left burning in rooms no one entered.

Each morning I crossed the wet field with a bucket of grain. The grass soaked my cuffs. The mountains, blue and administrative in the west, presided over everything with the calm of judges who had heard too much testimony to be moved. Crows worked the fence posts. Somewhere a tractor coughed itself awake. Never lifted his head, and the world gathered around that motion.

“Here,” I would say.

But what does here mean to an animal?

To a horse, perhaps, here is not a point on a map but a pressure in the air, a sweetness in the feed, the nearness of a hand. To a person, here is always contaminated by then. Here is a pasture, yes, but also a battlefield not far off, a road once traveled by men with rifles, a river that carried tobacco, rumor, bodies, law. Here is Virginia, where the land is beautiful in a way that feels almost guilty, as though beauty were an argument offered by the earth in its own defense.

Never chewed loudly, indifferently. He had no interest in my moral weather.

I envied him that.

Yet even animals inherit human arrangements. His pasture was bordered by split rail, by survey, by deed. He grazed on land that had passed through hands, some gloved, some chained, some soft with inheritance, some raw from labor. The grass grew anyway. This was not forgiveness. Grass is not forgiveness. It is merely the green persistence of the world, which must not be mistaken for absolution.

Once, in October, I tried to ride him.

The leaves had begun their annual rehearsal of fire. The air smelled of hay, damp bark, and something mineral rising from the creek. I set the saddle on his back with the careful incompetence of a penitent arranging flowers at a grave. Never stood still, too still. His skin trembled beneath the blanket. I tightened the girth, whispering nonsense—good boy, easy, easy—as if fear were a door that gentleness alone could open.

When I put my boot in the stirrup, he moved.

Not violently. Worse: deliberately. He stepped away from me with a precision that revealed the full ridiculousness of my intention. My foot swung in air. My hand clutched mane, leather, nothing. For one second I hung beside him like an unfinished thought, and then I fell into the mud.

Never looked back.

It is possible that philosophy begins in humiliation. Not the grand humiliations—war, plague, exile, the collapse of empires—but the small collapse of a body that had imagined itself in command. In the mud I understood, briefly, that fear is not always a warning. Sometimes it is a tutor. Sometimes it is the mind admitting that the world is not an extension of its will.

I lay there laughing, then not laughing.

Above me, the sky carried its pale, indifferent blue from horizon to horizon. A vulture circled so high it seemed less like a bird than a punctuation mark placed by God after an unfinished sentence. Never returned to grazing. The saddle sat crooked on his back, absurd as a crown on a saint.

After that I stopped trying to ride him.

Instead I walked beside him when he allowed it. We moved along the fence at dusk, past milkweed split open and releasing its ghostly silk, past the pond where frogs sounded their wet little hammers. Sometimes he lowered his head to the grass, and I stood with the lead rope slack in my hand, watching the evening enter the field by degrees. There was no conquest in it. No scene of mastery. Only proximity, which may be the most difficult form of love.

I began to think that Never was not a name but a discipline.

Never forget, says history, though it says it badly, with monuments and omissions, with plaques polished by weather and lies polished by repetition.

Never trust the frightened mind when it speaks of purity.

Never believe the pastoral is innocent.

Never put your faith in ownership.

Never assume the trembling will pass simply because the hand has steadied.

And yet: never turn away from the animal at the gate, who waits without symbolism, hungry in the morning.

Winter came down over Virginia quietly, first as frost whitening the trough, then as a hard glitter on the pasture. The fields lost their softness. The trees became anatomical, each branch a black vein against the morning. Never’s coat thickened. Steam rose from his nostrils when he breathed, and I loved him then with an ache almost impersonal, as one loves fire or bread or the voice of someone singing in another room.

Sometimes, placing hay in the rack, I pressed my palm against his neck. Beneath the winter hair: heat. Beneath the heat: the old engine of blood. Beneath the blood: whatever it is that goes on being itself without our permission.

I cannot say he trusted me. Trust is a human word and perhaps too dramatic. But there were mornings when he did not move away. Mornings when the fog lay low over the pasture and the barn seemed to float, loosened from history for a moment, though of course nothing is ever loosened from history. It merely grows quiet enough for us to pretend.

Never would stand beside me in that gray suspension, and I would feel fear still present, but changed. Not gone—fear rarely leaves the body it has educated—but altered into attention. A listening at the edge of the self.

In Virginia the past is never past, someone said, or should have said, or says daily without knowing. It grazes in the field. It flicks its tail at flies. It lowers its great head and eats from the earth. It lets you come close, some days. Other days it turns and runs, and the ground shakes with what you have not understood.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic, dreamlike monologue that begins with stalls labeled by names and develops into strange meditations on horses, mountains, guilt, and memory.
counterfactuals.output:
Stalls labeled by names: **Mara**, **Juniper**, **Saint**, **Bluebell**, **No One**.

I walked past them in the half-light, reading each small brass plate as if it were a sentence from a book I had once loved and then betrayed. The stable breathed in its sleep. Straw shivered underfoot. Somewhere a horse moved its great, patient weight from one leg to another, and the sound was like a mountain remembering that it had once been an animal.

I do not know why the stall marked **No One** was open.

Inside, there was only a rope, a salt block worn into the shape of a moon, and the smell of rain that had not yet fallen. I stood there with my hands in my pockets, guilty as a child who has hidden a broken cup behind the stove. Guilty of what? Of leaving. Of returning. Of having a body that insists on being carried through the world while the soul keeps asking to lie down in the grass.

Horses know something about forgiveness, but they never say it plainly. They lower their dark heads to the trough. They flick flies from their flanks with the elegance of queens dismissing ministers. Their eyes hold the long horizontal sorrow of fields, roads, fences, wars, weddings, children growing taller than their mothers. They have pulled our carts, borne our dead, fled our fires, stood steaming in winter while men decided the fates of countries. Still, in dreams, they come when called.

The mountains beyond the stable were blue and enormous, asleep beneath their blankets of pine. I used to believe mountains were proof that the earth had wanted to rise, that it had strained upward toward heaven and then hardened in the act. Now I think they are the backs of ancient horses lying down under the world, too tired to carry us any farther.

When I was young, I touched a horse’s neck and felt beneath the skin the thunder of its heart. I thought: here is a cathedral with hooves. Here is a storm that lets itself be brushed. I did not yet understand that gentleness is often the costume worn by strength, or that memory, like a horse, can startle at the smallest movement.

There are things I have not forgiven myself for. They follow me softly, nose to shoulder, through the dusk. They stand outside my window at night, breathing clouds onto the glass. Sometimes I wake certain I have heard them in the hallway—the slow knock of hooves, the shifting of old grief. I turn on the lamp, and the room is only a room: chair, book, water glass, the pale square of a mirror holding my face as if it were evidence.

But memory is not evidence. Memory is weather. It gathers, it breaks, it gilds the wrong hill. It puts a white horse where there was only fog. It makes a mother’s hand larger than it was, a door smaller, a farewell endless. It lets the dead speak in voices they never used while living. It changes the labels on the stalls.

**Mara** becomes **Mercy**.  
**Juniper** becomes **Return**.  
**Saint** becomes **Hunger**.  
**Bluebell** becomes **The Year I Could Not Sleep**.  
And **No One**—poor open, empty **No One**—becomes my own name.

I entered that stall as if entering a chapel. The straw was cool. Dust swam in the gold light. I pressed my palm against the wooden wall and felt, or imagined I felt, the warmth left by an absent animal. How strange, to be comforted by what has already gone. How human, to build a house for absence and then kneel inside it.

Outside, the mountains darkened. Their ridges looked like the folded wings of something too vast to rise. A horse whinnied, or perhaps it was the wind crossing a pass. For a moment, I could not tell whether I was in the stable, or the stable was in me—each stall a chamber, each name a wound, each sleeping beast a memory I had tried to tame.

I wanted to say I am sorry.

Not to anyone in particular. To the horses. To the mountains. To the child I had been, who believed every path led home if followed long enough. To the dead, who had become so quiet that I mistook their silence for peace. To the living, whom I had loved imperfectly, which is to say, as well as I could.

The open stall waited.

I stood there until dawn began to loosen the world from its dream. The brass plates brightened one by one. In the east, the mountains lifted their long blue heads. And somewhere beyond the fields, beyond the fences, beyond the last road I could name, something ran—not away, not toward, but simply ran, carrying the whole trembling morning in its mane.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a dense avant-garde prose poem involving horse stables, a chestnut gelding called Never, Panther Gap, and the line “I first mistook gelding for gilding.”
counterfactuals.output:
In the horse stables the dusk curdled into a brown sacrament, warm with ammonia, oats, bitten rope, the soft litigation of hooves against boards. A chestnut gelding called Never stood in the last stall as if time had been rubbed down and cinched to his breathing. His flank shone like a door left open in a burning orchard. I first mistook gelding for gilding. Forgive me: language had already begun its rust-colored sabotage, every word wearing a bridle of another word, every body revised by the hand that names it.

Beyond the stable roof, Panther Gap opened and closed its black mouth. The hills there did not rise; they listened. Wind moved through them like a rumor of claws. Never lifted his head, and the whole corridor of stalls became an instrument: latch-click, hay-dust, leather-sigh, the wet green thunder of chewing. In his eye I saw a small inverted weather: my face, a lantern, a nail, the Gap, the Gap’s pantherless hunger. Nothing leapt, and so everything was leaping.

I wanted to saddle him with negation and ride until the map confessed its animal error. Never, Never, I whispered, and the name returned not as refusal but as pasture: a word where the fence had rotted through. He stamped once. The floor remembered forests. The stable remembered lightning. My hands smelled of apples and iron. In Panther Gap, night unbuttoned its pelt, and the gelding, ungilded, unkinged, immense in his lack, breathed gold from the dark without keeping any for himself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal stable scene in the style of contemporary lyric prose, including odd horse names, wordplay, rural Virginia, and an unsettling final image about a gold door.
counterfactuals.output:
In rural Virginia, where the hills lay down like tired green animals and the evening came on smelling of hay, rain, and old pennies, the stable kept its own weather.

Inside, the horses stood in their stalls as if waiting for instructions from another century. There was a mare named Weather Tax, a skewbald gelding called Saint Rutabaga, and a nervous little roan the children had christened Maybe Later. In the last stall, half in shadow, half in straw-light, slept a long-faced creature named Sir Not-Appearing, who never came when called but was always there when no one wanted him.

The rafters creaked in fluent barn. Swallows stitched blue thread through the dusk. A pitchfork leaned against the wall like punctuation after a sentence no one had survived. Everywhere, the stable made its small arguments: oats versus throat, hoof versus proof, mane versus meaning. The farmhand, a girl with rain in her pockets, said the horses understood puns better than people because horses were already half metaphor—four legs, one sorrow, and a door-shaped longing in the chest.

Beyond the open doors, the Blue Ridge floated in a bowl of violet. Cows moved through the pasture like slow thoughts. Somewhere near Charlottesville, a tractor coughed itself into prayer. The creek behind the barn kept saying over and over what water says when it has nothing new to confess.

At night, the horses dreamed loudly. Weather Tax kicked at invisible invoices. Saint Rutabaga whinnied hymns through a mouth full of roots. Maybe Later pressed his soft muzzle to the latch and whispered no, not yet, not yet. Sir Not-Appearing opened one black eye and looked at the far wall, where the boards had begun to glow.

By morning, a door had formed there.

Not a wooden door. Not a barn door. A gold door, narrow and tall, fitted into the stable wall as neatly as a secret in a family Bible. No hinges, no knob—only a warm metallic surface that reflected nothing correctly. In it, the horses appeared standing upright. The girl appeared old. The fields outside appeared underwater.

And when the sun rose over rural Virginia, bright as a bitten coin, the gold door opened inward just enough to show a darkness full of hay, breathing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
